## Hypothesis: There is a relationship between changes in property crime and violent crime.
## Null hypothesis: There is no significant correlation between violent_pct_change and property_pct_change.
## Alternative hypothesis: There is a significant correlation between violent_pct_change and property_pct_change.

```{r }
# This part of the code makes new columns that show crime rates. vI took crime numbers in each city and divided them by the city’s population. Afterward,I  multiplied it by 1,000. It tells me how many crimes happen for every 1,000 people,"
```



```{r }

md_city_change <- md_city_rates %>%
  mutate(
    violent_pct_change = ((violent_rate_2020 - violent_rate_2019) / violent_rate_2019) * 100,
    property_pct_change = ((property_rate_2020 - property_rate_2019) / property_rate_2019) * 100
  )
"My code shows how much crime went up or down from 2019 to 2020 per city"

md_city_change %>%
  summarise(
    mean_2020   = mean(violent_rate_2020, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_2020 = median(violent_rate_2020, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_2020    = min(violent_rate_2020, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_2020    = max(violent_rate_2020, na.rm = TRUE))
 "This code tells us what violent crime looked like across all Maryland cities in 2020."

md_city_change %>%
  summarise(
    sd_violent_change = sd(violent_pct_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_property_change = sd(property_pct_change, na.rm = TRUE)
  )


# My code shows how different the percent changes were between cities."

""


```

```{r }
cor_result <- cor.test(
  md_city_change$violent_pct_change,
  md_city_change$property_pct_change
)
md_city_change %>%
  mutate(z_violent = scale(violent_pct_change)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(z_violent)))

md_city_change <- md_city_change %>%
  mutate(prop_group = if_else(property_rate_2020 >= median(property_rate_2020),
                              "High property crime",
                              "Low property crime"))


 
```

```{r }
cor.test(md_city_change$violent_pct_change, md_city_change$property_pct_change)

md_summary <- md_city_change |>
  summarize(
    violent_mean = mean(violent_pct_change),
    property_mean = mean(property_pct_change),
    violent_sd = sd(violent_pct_change),
    property_sd = sd(property_pct_change),
    correlation = cor(violent_pct_change, property_pct_change),
    p_value = cor.test(violent_pct_change, property_pct_change)$p.value
  )



# My code checks if changes in violent crime and changes in property crime are really connected or if the pattern we see is just random, using a p-valu" I fixed errors by re-running the mutate step before I ran the tests and making sure my variable names were correct."

md_city_change <- md_city_change %>%
  mutate(prop_group = if_else(property_rate_2020 >= median(property_rate_2020),
                              "High property crime",
                              "Low property crime"))


t.test(violent_rate_2020 ~ prop_group, data = md_city_change)

# The t test found a very strong difference between the two groups (p-value near zero). The test shows that cities with increases in property crime also had different violent crime changes Because of this, my claim is supported and the null hypothesis is rejected. 


```
 
 

Even though the correlation test was statistically significant, the relationship is weak. Violent and property crime tend to move in the same direction, but only a little, which is why the trend line rises slightly even though the points are scattered.

 The p-value was below 0.05, so I reject the null hypothesis and can see that the changes in property crime and violent crime are related.


1.The data shows violent and property crime count with population totals for Maryland cities, covering the years 2019 and 2020.

2.The most important columns are the ones showing change over time like  specifically violent_pct_change and property_pct_change.

3. The data is missing context variables such as demographics, and policing data, both  of which can have implications on the numbers.

4.Using the violent_rate_2020 column, I  noticed that the mean was 2.90, the median was 1.77, the lowest value was 0, and the highest value was 23.97

Story Idea: 
Covid-19 wasn’t a reliable indicator of whether crime rates went up or down across Maryland

The Covid-19 pandemic didn’t make crime rise or fall the same way across Maryland. Some places saw big change, others stayed about the same. Crime data released by police indicates that covid19 was not a good way to predict what would happen to crime in different communities.
 
 Certin Maryland cities had violent crime rates as low as 0, others reached almost 24 crimes per 1,000 people. The percent changes also moved in vastly different directions. A few places saw crime go up by more than 100 percent, while others saw a drop. Most cities stayed closer to zero, with only small changes.
